one_liner: HotSpot (Temurin 27) and GraalVM JIT split and count a 50,000-word text 1.25-1.4x faster than every C and C++ build in LangArena Etc::Words.
what_it_does: A LangArena benchmark task, not a library. Each iteration splits a 325 KB text of 50,000 space-separated lowercase words, counts word frequencies in a fresh hash map, scans for the most frequent word, and folds its count, its djb2 hash and the vocabulary size into a checksum. The Java side (java/src/main/java/benchmarks/Words.java) is a few lines: text.split(" "), HashMap<String,Integer> with getOrDefault plus put, and a loop over entrySet. Nothing here can be linked into a C++ program; the row is evidence about the JVM, not a component to adopt.
how_it_is_fast: The win comes from the libraries and the allocator, not from JIT code generation. String.split with a one-character, non-regex delimiter takes the JDK's fast path (an indexOf loop plus substring copies, no java.util.regex). Each String caches its hashCode, so the second lookup (put after getOrDefault) does not re-hash, and counts of 1-9 come from the Integer cache, so boxing allocates nothing. Map nodes and substrings are bump-allocated in a TLAB and dropped wholesale by the young-generation GC. The C++ baseline instead uses std::istringstream, which copies the whole text into its stringbuf every iteration and builds a sentry plus a locale ctype whitespace test for every operator>> extraction. It inserts 18,623 nodes into a std::unordered_map<std::string,int> with no reserve and frees them all at the end of each timed iteration. Ahead-of-time compiled Zig, Crystal, Rust, Go and C# AOT also beat every C++ row, so this is not a JIT-specific effect (results file).
when_to_use: Deciding whether a JVM log-processing, tokenizing or word-count job needs a C++ rewrite: idiomatic Java beat the idiomatic istringstream plus unordered_map C++ in all five monthly runs (2026-07-14 to 2026-10-05).
Long-running JVM services or batch jobs that tokenize on a single ASCII delimiter and count a modest vocabulary (about 18.6k distinct 3-8 letter keys here) where the map fits in cache.
Any JVM GC setup: all five Java rows (G1, ParallelGC 'Opt', SerialGC -Xmx512m, GraalVM CE JIT and GraalVM Serial) finished in 0.974-1.38 s, all faster than the best C++ row at 1.587 s.
As a reference for how much a stream-based C++ tokenizer gives away compared with a split-into-substrings approach.
when_not_to_use: Memory-tight jobs: peak RSS was 309 MB for Java/OpenJDK and 445 MB for GraalVM JIT, against 7.8 MB for C++/G++ and 5.1 MB for C/Gcc.

When you control the C++ code: the slow parts are istringstream and a node-based map. A std::string_view splitter with a flat or open-addressing map was never measured (inference), and in the same file Zig/Unchecked (0.57 s), Crystal (0.88 s) and Rust (1.021 s) beat Java with a few MB of RSS.

General text: split(" ") splits on the single space character only, while operator>> splits on any locale whitespace (tabs, newlines). Both give the same counts here only because the generated text uses single spaces.
One-shot command-line runs: the suite excludes JVM startup and a 72-iteration warm-up from timing; a single-pass word count would pay JVM start and JIT compilation.
Results quoted as a JIT advantage: C# AOT (1.397-1.399 s) matched C# JIT (1.422 s), and the category label 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' does not fit this test.

integration.dependencies: A JDK (Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 or GraalVM CE 25.0.4.1.1 measured); only java.util is used by the task (the harness reads its config with org.json)
integration.min_toolchain: Java 21 bytecode (pom.xml source/target 21); measured on Temurin 27+35 and GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1, both with -Xmx2g
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X); any JVM platform in principle
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded; the HashMap is local to each run() call

gotchas: The workload is a small-vocabulary hash test. The suite's LCG (IM 139968) repeats, so the 50,000-word text is an 18,656-word block repeated about 2.7 times, with 18,623 distinct words (all 3-8 letters, within libstdc++'s 15-byte small-string buffer) and one clear winner ('tea', 9 times). My Python replay reproduces run.js's checksum 1998586832 over 432 iterations (72 warm-up plus 360 timed). The C/C++ integer next_int formula and Java's floating-point one produce byte-identical texts, so every language does the same work.

The Java code does more hash-map work than the C++ code, not less: getOrDefault then put is two lookups per word against C++'s single try_emplace. It still wins because the second lookup reuses the String's cached hash and the C++ cost sits in istream extraction and per-node malloc/free.

No configuration got real LTO: cpp/Makefile passes -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only on the link line, and the objects are compiled without -flto. That hardly matters here, because the hot code is libstdc++ templates and istream calls inside words.cpp.

One in-process timing per configuration with no variance. The direction has held for five months (Java/OpenJDK 1.09-1.25x ahead of the best C/C++ row; GraalVM JIT 1.03x in July and August, 1.29-1.38x since September), but the margin moves by about 15% between runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Use this row specifically for JVM-versus-C++ tokenize-and-count; the separately catalogued Crystal Etc::Words row (0.88 s) is faster with 8.8 MB RSS if the language is open. The LuaJIT word-count gist and LuaJIT k-nucleotide siblings show the same std::unordered_map<std::string,int> weakness, but with one-run, older evidence; this LangArena row has public code, flags and five monthly reruns.
verified_claims_summary: In the 2026-10-05 LangArena run on an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X under Linux, Temurin OpenJDK 27 (default G1, -Xmx2g) took 1.272 s for 360 timed iterations of splitting and counting a 50,000-word text. That compares with 1.587 s for the best of 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ builds (C++/G++/PGO, GCC 16.0.1 trunk, libstdc++ istringstream and unordered_map) and 1.638 s for C++/G++ at -O2: about 1.25x and 1.29x faster (derived from page data). GraalVM CE 25 JIT took 1.15 s (about 1.38x).
status_note: Active MIT-licensed suite (41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, monthly reruns; Words.java unchanged since it was added on 2026-02-28). The author calls the suite subjective and says AI tools helped port the tasks, so treat the row as a language-level data point, not code to adopt.
